CNC Machining is like three jobs.

First is the building of the fixtures for making parts. I compare this part to legos; you usually use the same basic components in different arrangements (lathes are trivial, usually - just different jaws), and there is definitely value in being able to build and break down the fixtures quickly, so as to change the production runs between different parts with minimal downtime.

Second is the design of the program, which requires you to have a copy of the G&M compiler inside your head. If regular computer programming is something you enjoy, you should learn the language(s) with no problems - and it is definitely a salable skill to have. Multiaxis work, requiring CAD/CAM modeling, is a different skill from the basic stuff, but it comes down to imagining how you would make the part by hand, and then getting the machine to make it for you.

Thirdly is actually running the machine. You need to be able to use the measuring tools - calipers, mikes, gauges, etc. etc. etc. - to maintain the dimensions within tolerance, to be mindful of the machine and to make adjustments to the tool offsets to adjust for wear and variation in the parts, to be knowledgeable of how to cut the materials you will be working with - knowing what speeds/feeds to use, knowing about metallurgy, knowing how to use the machinists reference handbook - and being really, really quick and accurate at swapping the stock or castings in and out of the machine and keeping busy while the parts are running.

All in all, I really enjoyed it, and I won't be sad if I go back to it after I write my novel.
